title: The Soaked Ledger

beats.t: In the lowest chamber of the twelfth house, where the loom threads ended, a black tiger lay prone. A chain dangled from the golden ring around its neck.
Every so often, the chain pulled. Each time, the tiger slid another handspan downward. Its claws scored long marks in the floor.
A little longer. Just hold on a little longer.
Even the tiger didn't know whom it was speaking to. Beneath its forepaws lay a ledger, its cover drenched.
The ledger opened by itself. An unfamiliar page lay among familiar entries. The handwriting was unmistakably its own. Only when it had written it was missing from memory.
When did I write this?
The first line held a date. Spring. The numbers had blurred beyond reading. Beneath them, one line: Bus stop. Rain. Half an umbrella.
A bus stop. That child offered an umbrella at a bus stop last time too. Near our apartments, on that rainy day.
The tiger shook its head. The same scene overlapped twice: one from this life, one it didn't remember. They looked exactly alike.
The ledger never lies. My one source of pride.
As it read, the rain grew louder. The ledger became a window. Beyond it stood an old bus stop.
A girl in a school uniform stood drenched, water dripping from her hair. Beside her, another girl tilted half an umbrella over her.
It's that girl.
The girl with the umbrella smiled. Let's share. Half each. She didn't care that her own shoulder was getting wet.
The drenched girl couldn't speak. In all her memory, that was the only day someone had offered her something without wanting anything back.
I know her. Even if her name won't come, I know her.
The bus arrived, and they boarded together. The girl with the umbrella took a packet of gummies from her bag and handed over half. Without counting. Without thinking.
The drenched girl held the gummies for a long time without eating them. They were too precious. She didn't know how to repay what she'd received.
I bought an umbrella and went back the next day to repay her. She only smiled and said she already had one.
A tiny doodle marked the ledger's corner: two clumsy umbrellas. Beside them were the erased remains of Received and To Repay.
The ledger turned. Seasons passed. The two girls waited for the bus together every day. The umbrella was always half each.
The drenched girl began working part-time. A convenience store, dawn leaflet rounds, a restaurant on weekends. She saved the money in an envelope. On the front she wrote: Go to the sea together.
I said we should see the sea. She had never seen it before.
The envelope grew thicker. Whenever the girl with the umbrella heard about it, she clapped. I'll save too. Half each.
Half each, she always said. Umbrellas, sweets, the sea. She set aside my share before counting her own.
The tiger read those words aloud. Its throat tightened afterward, as though these weren't words in a ledger but words it had heard from someone long ago.
Why would a girl like that act differently only that day?
The rain intensified as though answering. Water spilled over the bus-stop roof. The tiger was afraid to turn the page. Still, it pushed the paper with a paw.
Then the final page. The same bus stop. The same girl holding an umbrella. But she wasn't smiling. She didn't offer the umbrella.
She snatched something from the drenched girl's hand: the envelope holding money saved for so long. Then she turned away.
Yes. This is what I remember. The day she abandoned me.
But the picture in the ledger trembled once. The turning girl's face briefly twisted into something unfamiliar.
…What was that just now?
It tried to look again. The picture had already blurred, as though rainwater had chosen that entry alone to erase.
She was strange that day. She always had a nickname for me, yet she didn't call me by name.
The tiger pressed the ledger with a forepaw, afraid to extend its claws in case the wet paper tore. It stared at that entry for a long time.
What if it wasn't her? No. What would that make everything I've done?
It couldn't finish. The ring around its neck tightened once, cutting off its breath. As though ordering it to stop thinking.
Close the old ledger. Wet paper lies.
Chairman. In that child's eyes just now...
What you saw was rain. Rain blurs everything. Like you.
The chain jerked hard. The tiger fell flat. The ledger slid from under its paws. It twisted its body and gathered the book against its chest.
Go down. In the sky of twenty-seven moons, I will give you your final task. Empty that child.
I have been. All along. But why do you grow fuller the emptier she becomes?
You have learned to count. Needlessly.
That was the only answer. The chain snapped downward. Loom threads tore apart to make a passage. Red starlight rose from below.
Even as it fell, the tiger refused to let go of the ledger. Its wet cover clung to its chest. Only the little note tucked inside retained its warmth.
If I could see that half-shared umbrella once more, I'd know.
The wind blew upward. Below, red threads glittered like stars. Between them appeared the roof of an ancient temple. Twenty-seven moons floated above it.
I'll meet her again down there, won't I? What will you order me to take this time?
Everything. Even what she holds on to until the end.
What she holds on to until the end is a notebook. Filled with other people's names.
There was no answer from above. The tiger held the soaked ledger closer. An unfamiliar feeling stirred beneath the ring around its neck. A feeling called doubt.
The red sky swallowed her. Above, the twelfth-house door closed quietly.
